data.title: B2 Progress Check
data.description: A second mixed grammar and usage check to measure progress and confirm whether the learner is working securely at CEFR B2 level.

sections.explain: In past narration, use the past perfect continuous for an earlier ongoing action: 'had been travelling'. 'has been' is present perfect, and 'had been travel' lacks the -ing form.

words.word: She was tired because she had been travel all day.
She was tired because she had been travelling all day.
She was tired because she has been travelling all day.

sections.explain: Indirect questions use statement word order: 'where the station is'. We don't invert ('where is the station') or add 'does'.

words.word: Could you tell me where is the station?
Could you tell me where the station is?
Could you tell me where does the station is?

sections.explain: With musical instruments in a general sense, use 'the': 'plays the violin'. Omitting the article or using 'a' breaks the meaning.

words.word: He plays a violin beautifully.
He plays the violin beautifully.
He plays violin beautifully.

sections.explain: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: 'Each of the students has'. The verb isn't plural, and the noun must be plural.

words.word: Each of the student has a laptop.
Each of the students have a laptop.
Each of the students has a laptop.

sections.explain: Non-gradable (extreme) adjectives like 'impossible' take 'absolutely', not 'very': 'absolutely impossible'. 'more impossible' also doesn't work with an absolute adjective.

words.word: It was very impossible to hear.
It was absolutely more impossible to hear.
It was absolutely impossible to hear.

sections.explain: The fixed phrase is 'on purpose' (deliberately): 'She did it on purpose'. 'in purpose' and 'by purpose' are not correct.

words.word: She did it on purpose.
She did it by purpose.
She did it in purpose.

sections.explain: 'Admit' is followed by the -ing form: 'admitted stealing'. 'admitted to steal' and 'admitted steal' are incorrect.

words.word: He admitted steal the money.
He admitted stealing the money.
He admitted to steal the money.

sections.explain: We 'take responsibility' in English: this is the standard collocation. 'make/do responsibility' are not used.

words.word: The company will do responsibility for the error.
The company will make responsibility for the error.
The company will take responsibility for the error.

sections.explain: 'That said' is a fixed discourse marker meaning 'nevertheless': 'That said, there were some positives'. 'That saying' and 'That is said' are not correct.

words.word: The results were poor. That said, there were some positives.
The results were poor. That is said, there were some positives.
The results were poor. That saying, there were some positives.

sections.explain: In an it-cleft emphasising a person, use 'who' (or 'that'): 'It was John who broke the window'. 'which' is for things, and the relative pronoun can't be omitted here.

words.word: It was John broke the window.
It was John which broke the window.
It was John who broke the window.
